questions.question: Which semantic landmark element must appear only once as visible content per HTML document?
questions.explanation: There must not be more than one visible <main> element in a document according to the W3C specification.

questions.question: Which element is best suited for a self-contained blog post that makes sense on its own?
questions.explanation: <article> represents an independent, self-contained piece of content like a blog post or news story.

questions.question: Which tag represents content tangentially related to the content around it, such as a sidebar or pull quote?
questions.explanation: <aside> represents content tangentially related to the content around it, typically rendered as a sidebar.

questions.question: What is the primary accessibility benefit of semantic landmark elements?
options: They allow screen reader users to jump directly to specific sections like navigation or main content
questions.hint: Screen readers can skip directly to landmarks.
questions.explanation: Assistive technologies allow users to navigate directly between landmark elements (<nav>, <main>, <aside>, etc.).

questions.question: When should a generic <div> be used instead of a semantic <section> or <article>?
options: When an element is needed purely for CSS styling or layout wrapping without semantic meaning
questions.explanation: <div> has no semantic meaning and is appropriate when grouping elements strictly for styling, scripting, or layout.
